definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Practice: together with dispassion (vairāgya) the means by which the restless mind is held (6.35); the 'former practice' (pūrva-abhyāsa) of a previous life carries the fallen yogin onward (6.44).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The counter-order whose rise, together with the decline of dharma, is the occasion on which the Lord sends himself forth (4.7).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Said by Kṛṣṇa of himself: though unborn and of imperishable self, and lord of beings, he comes into being through his own māyā (4.6).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Ignorance, which covers knowledge and so deludes creatures (5.15); destroyed by knowledge of the self, after which knowledge illumines the highest (5.16); the source of the doubt lodged in the heart (4.42); the ignorant one (ajña) perishes (4.40).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: One of the three things to be understood along with action (karma) and vikarma (4.17); even sages are bewildered about it (4.16); the wise one sees inaction in action and action in inaction (4.18); the unattached one 'does nothing at all' though engaged in action (4.20).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The remainder of the sacrifice is called amṛta; those who eat it go to the eternal Brahman (4.31).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: One of the two paired breaths: some offer prāṇa into apāna and apāna into prāṇa (4.29); prāṇa and apāna moving within the nostrils are to be made even (5.27). The chapters do not define the direction of each.
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: the meditating yogin is to be without possessions (aparigraha) (6.10); cf. the one who has given up all possessions (tyakta-sarva-parigraha) and incurs no fault (4.21).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The state of not coming back (to birth), reached by those whose intellect, self and goal are That and whose impurities are shaken off by knowledge (5.17).

literal: offering; that by which one offers

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: In 4.24 the offering (or the means of offering) is itself Brahman.
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The sage who wishes to ascend to yoga, for whom action (karma) is said to be the means (6.3); contrasted with the one who has ascended (yogārūḍha).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The firm seat set up in a clean place, neither too high nor too low, spread with kuśa grass, deer-skin and cloth, on which the meditating yogin sits (6.11–12), holding body, head and neck in line (6.13). In these chapters āsana is the seat, not a series of postures.

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Used both reflexively (oneself, one's own mind: 'one should raise the self by the self', the self as its own friend or enemy, 6.5–6) and for the self in which all beings are seen (4.35, 6.29), in which the controlled mind rests (6.18, 6.25) and which is seen by the self (6.20); the yoked yogin's self has become the self of all beings (5.7).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Seeing the same everywhere, pleasure or pain, by the measure of oneself; the yogin who does this is held to be the highest (6.32).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Arjuna's being Kṛṣṇa's devotee and friend is the stated reason he receives the ancient yoga, the highest secret (4.3).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The noun does not occur in chs. 4–6, but the verb bhaj- does: the Lord 'responds to' (bhajāmi) people in the way they approach him (4.11); the yogin established in oneness worships (bhajati) him as abiding in all beings (6.31); the one who worships (bhajate) him with faith and inner self fixed on him is the most yoked (6.47).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Enjoyments born of contact (saṃsparśaja bhoga) are wombs of sorrow, having a beginning and an end; the wise one does not delight in them (5.22).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The goal attained by the yogin who has inner happiness, delight and light and has become Brahman (5.24), by seers whose impurities are destroyed and dualities cut, devoted to the welfare of all beings (5.25); it is near on every side for self-knowing ascetics free of desire and anger (5.26). Cf. 'peace culminating in nirvāṇa, abiding in me' (6.15).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The boundless happiness that the stainless yogin, constantly yoking himself, easily enjoys (6.28).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Said of the yogin with inner happiness who attains brahma-nirvāṇa (5.24), and of the tranquil, stainless yogin with rajas stilled to whom supreme happiness comes (6.27).
Bhagavad Gītā 6.14: the meditator is to be firm in the vow of the brahmacārin (brahmacāri-vrata).

literal: the conduct of a (Vedic) student; celibacy

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The meditating yogin is to be firm in the vow of the brahmacārin (brahmacāri-vrata) (6.14).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: every factor of the sacrifice is Brahman and Brahman is to be reached by one absorbed in action as Brahman (4.24); sacrifice is offered into the fire of Brahman (4.25) and the sacrifices are spread 'in the mouth of Brahman' (4.32); eaters of the sacrifice's remainder go to the eternal Brahman (4.31); the yoked sage soon reaches Brahman (5.6); actions are 'placed in Brahman' (5.10); Brahman is flawless and the same, and those whose mind rests in sameness are established in it (5.19–20).

Bhagavad Gītā 4.24: the offering (or instrument of offering) is Brahman, the oblation is Brahman, offered by Brahman into the fire that is Brahman; Brahman is reached by one absorbed in action as Brahman.
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Steady in intellect, undeluded, neither rejoicing at the pleasant nor agitated by the unpleasant, established in Brahman (5.20).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: One of the instruments with which yogins act for self-purification (5.11); the intellect held in firmness (dhṛti) by which the mind is gradually brought to rest (6.25); the boundless happiness is 'grasped by the buddhi' beyond the senses (6.21); the fallen yogin regains the connection with understanding (buddhi-saṃyoga) of his former body (6.43); sama-buddhi = equal regard (6.9).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Created by the Lord according to the division of guṇa and karma, though he is the imperishable non-doer (4.13).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The mind to be restrained and made one-pointed in meditation (6.10, 6.12); when thoroughly controlled it rests in the self alone (6.18), like a lamp in a windless place (6.19); restrained (niruddha) by the practice of yoga it comes to rest (6.20).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The embodied one who, having renounced all actions by the mind, dwells at ease in the city of nine gates, neither acting nor causing action (5.13).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Deities to whom people sacrifice desiring quick success of their actions in the human world (4.12).
Bhagavad Gītā 4.7–8: dharma, whose decline together with the rise of adharma is the occasion of the Lord's coming into being, and whose firm establishment is one of its purposes, age after age.
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The firmness in which the intellect is held while the mind is gradually brought to rest (6.25).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Sacrifice made with material things (4.28), declared inferior to the sacrifice of knowledge (4.33).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Contact-born enjoyments are wombs of sorrow (5.22); yoga destroys sorrow for one measured in food, rest and effort (6.17); in the state of yoga one is not shaken even by heavy sorrow (6.22); yoga is defined as the unyoking from union with sorrow (duḥkha-saṃyoga-viyoga) (6.23).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The pairs such as cold and heat, pleasure and pain, honour and dishonour (6.7); one who has gone beyond them (dvandvātīta) is not bound though acting (4.22); one free of them (nirdvandva) is easily released from bondage (5.3).
Bhagavad Gītā 6.12: seated on the seat, making the mind one-pointed, one should practise yoga for purification of the self.
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Established in oneness, the yogin worships the Lord as abiding in all beings and abides in him however he lives (6.31).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The division of guṇas and actions according to which the Lord made the fourfold class-order (4.13); the guṇas are not further explained in chs. 4–6 (rajas is named in 6.27).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: In 4.24 the oblation is Brahman.

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The senses are offered into the fires of restraint and their actions into the fire of self-restraint (4.26–27); they are to be restrained to gain knowledge (4.39) and in meditation (6.12, 6.24); the knower holds that 'the senses move among the sense-objects' (5.9).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: the yoked knower holds that the senses move among the objects of the senses (indriyārtheṣu) (5.9); one attached neither to the objects of the senses nor to actions has ascended to yoga (6.4).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Kṛṣṇa is lord of beings though unborn (4.6), and great lord of all the worlds (sarva-loka-maheśvara), enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities and friend of all beings, knowing whom one attains peace (5.29).

Bhagavad Gītā 4.33–42 and 5.15–17: knowledge — learned from knowers who have seen the truth through prostration, questioning and service (4.34); by it one is not deluded again and sees all beings in the self and in the Lord (4.35); a raft across all wrong (4.36); a fire that burns all actions (4.37); the supreme purifier, found within oneself in time by one perfected in yoga (4.38); obtained by the faithful, intent and sense-restrained, and followed by supreme peace (4.39); it cuts doubt like a sword (4.42). It is covered by ignorance, which deludes creatures; where ignorance is destroyed, knowledge illumines the highest like the sun (5.15–16). 6.8 pairs it with realized knowledge (vijñāna).
Bhagavad Gītā 4.28, 4.33: the sacrifice of knowledge, offered by ascetics of strict vows; better than sacrifice made of material things, since all action without exception culminates in knowledge.
Bhagavad Gītā 4.19, 4.37: the fire of knowledge, which burns up actions — the learned one's actions are burnt in it, and as a kindled fire turns firewood to ash, it turns all actions to ash.
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The knowers who see the truth and teach knowledge (4.34); in 6.46 the yogin is held greater than the jñānins.

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Impurity destroyed by sacrifice (4.30), shaken off by knowledge (5.17), destroyed in the seers who attain brahma-nirvāṇa (5.25); the yogin who has become Brahman is stainless (akalmaṣa, vigata-kalmaṣa) (6.27–28).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: undertakings free of desire mark the learned (4.19); the unyoked is bound through the drive of desire (5.12); the surge of desire and anger is to be withstood before leaving the body (5.23); brahma-nirvāṇa is near those free of desire and anger (5.26); desires born of intention are to be abandoned in meditation (6.24); the yoked one is free of craving for all desires (6.18).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Action is the central theme of chs. 4–6: its course is deep and must be understood together with vikarma and inaction (4.16–18); actions do not stain the Lord (4.14); the ancients seeking liberation acted (4.15); all sacrifices are born of action (4.32); all action culminates in knowledge (4.33) and is burned by the fire of knowledge (4.37); for one wishing to ascend to yoga action is the means (6.3); one should do the action that ought to be done without depending on its fruit (6.1).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The bondage from which one free of the pairs of opposites is easily released (5.3); the unyoked one, attached to fruit through desire, is bound (5.12); actions do not bind one who knows the Lord's freedom from them (4.14), the one beyond the pairs (4.22), or the one who has renounced actions by yoga and cut doubt by knowledge (4.41).

notes: The words in chs. 4–6 are bandha ('bondage', 5.3) and forms of the verb bandh- (badhyate 4.14; nibadhyate 4.22, 5.12; nibadhnanti 4.41); the compound karmabandha itself is 2.39's.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 5.2: the yoga of action, which together with renunciation brings the highest good and is superior to the renunciation of action; in 5.10–12 it is acting with actions placed in Brahman, abandoning attachment and the fruit, for purification of the self.

literal: giving up the fruit of action

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: expressed as abandoning attachment to the fruit of action (karmaphalāsaṅgaṃ tyaktvā, 4.20), giving up the fruit (karmaphalaṃ tyaktvā, 5.12, which brings lasting peace) and not depending on the fruit (anāśritaḥ karmaphalam, 6.1).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: the Lord is the maker (kartṛ) of the fourfold class order, yet is to be known as the non-doer (akartṛ), imperishable (4.13).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The lord creates neither agency nor actions for the world, nor the linking of action with its fruit; svabhāva is at work (5.14); the yoked knower thinks 'I do nothing at all', the senses moving among their objects (5.8–9).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Even kavis are bewildered about what action and inaction are (4.16).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: those free of passion, fear and anger came to the Lord's being (4.10); the surge of desire and anger is to be withstood (5.23); the ascetics free of desire and anger have brahma-nirvāṇa near (5.26); the sage from whom desire, fear and anger are gone is ever liberated (5.28).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Epithet of the yoked yogin who is satisfied with knowledge and realised knowledge and whose senses are conquered (6.8).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The state of the Lord, reached by many who were free of passion, fear and anger and purified by the austerity of knowledge (4.10).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The mind is restless, turbulent, strong and obstinate, as hard to restrain as the wind (6.34), but is held by practice and dispassion (6.35); it is to be made one-pointed (6.12), made to abide in the self (6.25) and brought back wherever it wanders (6.26); all actions are renounced 'by the mind' (5.13).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The one free of envy (vimatsara), content with what comes by chance, is not bound though acting (4.22).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: In 4.6 the Lord comes into being 'through his own māyā' (ātmamāyā) while presiding over his own prakṛti; chs. 4–6 do not define the word (commentators divide between a power of appearance and the Lord's will or knowledge).
Bhagavad Gītā 4.35: knowing which one does not again fall into delusion; 5.15: creatures are deluded because knowledge is covered by ignorance; 5.20: the knower of Brahman is undeluded.

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The sage intent on liberation (mokṣa-parāyaṇa), with senses, mind and intellect controlled and free of desire, fear and anger, is forever liberated (5.28); cf. the verbal forms 'you will be released' (mokṣyase 4.16, vimokṣyase 4.32).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: For the freed one acting for the sake of sacrifice, action dissolves entirely (4.23); the meditating sage free of desire, fear and anger is 'forever freed' (sadā mukta) (5.28).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The ancient seekers of liberation performed action, knowing the Lord's untainted relation to action (4.15).

Bhagavad Gītā 5–6: the sage yoked in yoga reaches Brahman soon (5.6); the sage intent on liberation, restrained in senses, mind and intellect, is ever free (5.28); the sage wishing to ascend to yoga has action as the means (6.3).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The body as the city of nine gates in which the self-controlled embodied one dwells at ease, neither acting nor causing action (5.13).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Arjuna thinks restraining (nigraha) the restless mind as very hard as restraining the wind (6.34); Kṛṣṇa grants that the mind is hard to restrain (durnigraha) but says it is held by practice and dispassion (6.35).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Both renunciation (saṃnyāsa) and the yoga of action bring about the highest good (5.2).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: without expectation (nirāśīḥ), with mind and self restrained and all possessions given up, one who does merely bodily action incurs no fault (4.21); the meditating yogin is to be alone, restrained in mind and self, without expectation and without possessions (6.10).

literal: free from the pairs of opposites

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: free of the pairs of opposites (nirdvandva), the constant renouncer is easily released from bondage (5.3); cf. dvandvātīta, 'gone beyond the pairs' (4.22).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The mind restrained by the practice of yoga, which comes to rest in the state called yoga (6.20).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The peace that culminates in nirvāṇa (nirvāṇa-paramā) and abides in the Lord, attained by the constantly yoked yogin (6.15); see brahma-nirvāṇa (5.24–26).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The wise call paṇḍita one whose undertakings are free of desire and intention and whose actions are burnt by the fire of knowledge (4.19); the paṇḍitas see all beings equally (5.18) and do not call Sāṃkhya and Yoga separate (5.4).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: For one who has conquered himself and is at peace, the paramātman is steadily composed amid cold and heat, pleasure and pain, honour and dishonour (6.7); the reading (the supreme self established in him, or his self supremely composed) is disputed.

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The succession through which the ancient yoga was received and known by the royal sages before being lost over time (4.2): Kṛṣṇa to Vivasvat, Vivasvat to Manu, Manu to Ikṣvāku (4.1).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: One who has given up all possessions (tyakta-sarva-parigraha), doing only bodily action, incurs no fault (4.21); the meditating yogin is without possessions (aparigraha) (6.10).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: One of three ways (with prostration and service) of approaching the truth-seeing knowers for knowledge (4.34).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: In 4.6 the Lord comes into being presiding over his own prakṛti (svāṃ prakṛtim adhiṣṭhāya).

Bhagavad Gītā 4.27–30, 5.27: the activities of prāṇa are offered into the fire of self-restraint (4.27); prāṇa is offered into apāna and apāna into prāṇa, and their movements restrained (4.29); those regulating food offer prāṇas into prāṇas (4.30); prāṇa and apāna moving within the nostrils are made equal (5.27).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Those intent on breath-regulation offer prāṇa into apāna and apāna into prāṇa, restraining their courses; this is one of the sacrifices (4.29).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Prostration before the truth-seeing knowers, with questioning and service, as the way to receive knowledge (4.34).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The ancient yoga now told to Arjuna is 'the highest secret' (4.3).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The royal sages who knew the yoga received through succession (4.2).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The yogin to whom supreme happiness comes has his rajas stilled (śānta-rajas) (6.27).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Seers whose impurities are destroyed, whose dualities are cut, who are self-restrained and devoted to the welfare of all beings, attain brahma-nirvāṇa (5.25).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Even one who merely wishes to know yoga passes beyond śabdabrahman (6.44); the chapter does not explain the term (commentators take it as the Veda).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: For one who has ascended to yoga (yogārūḍha), calm is said to be the means (6.3).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The learned see with an equal eye a learned brahmin, a cow, an elephant, a dog and a dog-eater (5.18); the yogin yoked in yoga, seeing the same everywhere (sama-darśana), sees the self in all beings and all beings in the self (6.29).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: In 4.24 'brahma-karma-samādhi' — concentration on (or absorption in) action as Brahman; the later technical yoga sense is not given in chs. 4–6 (cf. samāhita, 'composed', 6.7).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Sameness (sama, sāmya): being the same in success and failure (4.22); the mind established in sameness conquers creation here, because Brahman is flawless and the same (5.19); the yukta sees clod, stone and gold as the same (6.8) and has equal regard for friend and foe (6.9); Arjuna calls the yoga taught 'yoga as sāmya' (6.33).

Bhagavad Gītā 5.4–5: Sāṃkhya, which the childish, not the learned, call separate from Yoga; the place reached by the followers of Sāṃkhya is reached also by those of Yoga, and one who sees them as one sees. In context it stands with renunciation/knowledge.

Bhagavad Gītā 5–6: renunciation of actions (karma-saṃnyāsa) and the yoga of action both bring the highest good, the latter being superior (5.2); the constant renunciant (nitya-saṃnyāsin) is the one who neither hates nor desires (5.3); renunciation is hard to attain without yoga (5.6); the self-controlled embodied one renounces all actions with the mind (5.13); the renunciant is the one who does the required action without depending on its fruit, not the one without sacred fire or rites (6.1); what is called renunciation is yoga (6.2). 4.41 speaks of actions renounced through yoga.

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The constant renouncer (nitya-saṃnyāsin) is one who neither hates nor craves (5.3); the renouncer and yogin is one who does the action that ought to be done without depending on its fruit, not one without sacred fires or rites (6.1); 'renouncer of all intentions' marks the one ascended to yoga (6.4).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The doubting self perishes, with neither this world nor the next nor happiness (4.40); doubt born of ignorance and lodged in the heart is to be cut with the sword of knowledge (4.41–42); Arjuna asks Kṛṣṇa to cut his doubt about the fallen yogin (6.39).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Restraint of the senses: the senses are offered into the fires of restraint (4.26), and the actions of senses and breath into the fire of the yoga of self-restraint (ātma-saṃyama-yoga) kindled by knowledge (4.27). Not the technical saṃyama of the Yoga Sūtra.

notes: In the Gītā the word means restraint (of senses, mind), not the Yoga Sūtra's technical triad.

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Attachment to be abandoned in acting: abandoning attachment to the fruit of action (4.20); one whose attachment is gone (gata-saṅga) (4.23); acting having abandoned attachment (5.10–11).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: the learned one's undertakings are free of desire and intention (4.19); no one becomes a yogin without renouncing intention (6.2); the one who has ascended to yoga has renounced all intentions (6.4); desires arise from intention and are to be abandoned without remainder (6.24).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Supreme peace attained soon after gaining knowledge (4.39); lasting (naiṣṭhikī) peace for the yoked one who gives up the fruit (5.12); peace from knowing the Lord as enjoyer of sacrifices, lord of worlds and friend of all (5.29); peace culminating in nirvāṇa and abiding in the Lord (6.15).
Bhagavad Gītā 4.34: service, with prostration and questioning, by which knowledge is learned from the knowers of truth. 6.20 uses 'yoga-sevā' for the practice of yoga.
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The success of actions sought by those who sacrifice to deities, which comes quickly in the human world (4.12); the unbound one is the same in success and failure (4.22).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: External contacts (bāhya-sparśa) to which the self is unattached (5.21) and which are put outside in meditation (5.27); enjoyments born of contact are wombs of sorrow (5.22).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The one with faith, intent on it, with senses restrained, gains knowledge (4.39); the faithless perishes (4.40); Arjuna asks the fate of one endowed with faith who falls from yoga (6.37); the one who worships the Lord with faith is the most yoked (6.47).

Bhagavad Gītā 5–6: the happiness in the self, found by one unattached to external contacts, imperishable (5.21); enjoyments born of contact are sources of suffering (5.22); happiness, delight and light within (5.24); boundless happiness grasped by the intellect and beyond the senses (6.21); the highest happiness and the boundless happiness of contact with Brahman (6.27–28).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The lord creates neither agency nor actions nor the link of action and fruit; it is svabhāva that is at work (5.14).
Bhagavad Gītā 4.28: study/recitation offered as sacrifice by ascetics of strict vows, together with knowledge.

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Purified by the austerity of knowledge (jñāna-tapas) many came to the Lord's state (4.10); sacrifice by austerity (tapo-yajña) (4.28); the Lord is the enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities (5.29); the yogin is greater than ascetics (tapasvin) (6.46).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Knowing the Lord's birth and action 'in truth' (tattvataḥ) frees from rebirth (4.9); the knower of reality (tattvavit) thinks 'I do nothing' (5.8); established in the happiness of yoga one does not waver from reality (6.21); truth-seeing knowers teach (4.34).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The knowers who see the truth and will teach knowledge to one who approaches with prostration, questioning and service (4.34).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: the yoked knower of reality (tattvavit) thinks 'I do nothing at all' (5.8).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The truth-seeing knowers 'will instruct' (upadekṣyanti) knowledge to one who approaches rightly (4.34).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Yoga can be attained through the proper means by one whose self is controlled and who strives (6.36).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Together with practice, the means by which the restless mind is held (6.35).
Bhagavad Gītā 4.13: the fourfold class order (cāturvarṇya), created by the Lord according to the division of qualities (guṇa) and actions (karma).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The surge arising from desire and anger which the yoked, happy person withstands before release from the body (5.23).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Paired with knowledge: the yogin whose self is satisfied with jñāna and vijñāna is called yoked (6.8); chs. 4–6 do not distinguish the two (commentators take vijñāna as realised or specific knowledge).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Named in 4.17 as one of three things to be understood along with action and inaction; the text does not define it (commentators: prohibited action, or action of various kinds).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Sense-objects, sound and the rest, are offered into the fires of the senses (4.26); the senses move among the sense-objects (indriyārtha) (5.9); the one ascended to yoga is not attached to them (6.4).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: All wrongdoing, even of the worst evil-doer, is crossed by the raft of knowledge (4.36).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The wise one is content with what comes by chance (yadṛcchā-lābha) and is not bound though acting (4.22).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Sacrifice is extended in ch. 4: acting for the sake of sacrifice dissolves action (4.23); every factor of the rite is Brahman (4.24); many kinds are listed — to the gods, into Brahman, senses into restraint, objects into senses, actions of senses and breath into self-restraint, material goods, austerity, yoga, recitation and knowledge, breath-regulation, regulated food (4.25–30); all are born of action and destroy impurity (4.30, 4.32); the sacrifice of knowledge is best (4.33); the non-sacrificer has neither this world nor the next (4.31); the Lord is the enjoyer of sacrifices (5.29).
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The remainder of the sacrifice, called nectar; those who eat it go to the eternal Brahman (4.31; cf. 3.13).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Ascetics of strict vows sacrifice by recitation and knowledge (4.28); for self-knowing ascetics free of desire and anger brahma-nirvāṇa is near (5.26). Contrast 'ayati', one who does not strive (6.37).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: the imperishable yoga taught to Vivasvat and handed down to the royal sages (4.1–3); the yoga of action set beside renunciation and Sāṃkhya, which the wise see as one (5.1–6); what is called renunciation is yoga (6.2); the meditative yoking of the self in solitude (6.10–15); the state in which the restrained mind rests and the self is seen by the self (6.20–22), defined as 'the unyoking from union with sorrow' (6.23); called 'sāmya' (sameness) by Arjuna (6.33); the yogin is greater than ascetics, knowers and ritualists (6.46).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: One with faith who strays from yoga before perfection (6.37): he does not perish (6.40), dwells long in the worlds of the meritorious and is reborn among the pure and prosperous or among wise yogins (6.41–42), regains his former understanding and is carried on by former practice (6.43–44).

literal: one who has ascended to yoga

definitions.definition: Bhagavad Gītā 6.3–4: one who has ascended to yoga — when one is attached neither to sense objects nor to actions and has renounced all intentions; for him calm (śama) is said to be the means.
Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: The Lord comes into being 'age after age' (yuge yuge) to establish dharma (4.8).

Bhagavad Gītā 4–6: Used as a defining title: the one who sees inaction in action is yukta (4.18); the yukta knower thinks 'I do nothing' (5.8); gives up fruit and attains peace (5.12); withstands the surge of desire and anger (5.23); is satisfied with knowledge and sees clod and gold alike (6.8); his controlled mind rests in the self (6.18); 'measured' in food, rest, sleep and effort (6.17); the one who worships the Lord with faith is 'most yoked' (yukta-tama) (6.47).
